newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-Triad gang wars thrive in Hong Kong, Macau.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Triad gang wars thrive in Hong Kong, Macau.

text.p: A spate of firebombings, knifings and shootings in Hong Kong and Macau has aroused concern that "triad" crime gangs are getting out of hand as the two territories move towards Chinese rule.
But while the gangs send shivers down the spine of the common man, authorities doubt they pose any apocalyptic threat.
"At the end of the day they're just criminals out to make money," Detective Chief Inspector Ford McNicol of the Hong Kong police's anti-triad bureau said.

"Unfortunately there is an illusion surrounding triad activity, and the film industry and a certain way of portraying them is no good to the community of Hong Kong, and to our job of actually tackling the triads and organised crime," McNicol said.
Police know of about 50 triad groups in British-ruled Hong Kong. About 15 operate actively, counting several thousand members. "The majority are actually very badly organised," said McNicol.
TIT-FOR-TAT BOMBING
The firebombing of a karaoke nightclub in Hong Kong's Tsimshatsui district in late January was a deadly sign of rivalries between triad gangs battling for extortion profits.

The tit-for-tat bombing killed 17 people in what police described as a well-organised revenge attack in a quarrel between triad groups. They rounded up a clutch of suspects said to be linked to the Sun Yee On gang.
A spate of other blazes afterwards in bars, apartments and a squatter camp aroused speculation that the fires were linked.

The karaoke bar blaze and others like it may distort perceptions about the scale of triad violence but the threat is real enough. Last year a Hong Kong magazine editor was attacked in his office by gangsters who chopped off his arm and thumbs.
Attacks using meat cleavers and swords are common among triads. A hoard of such weapons was found at the burned-out karaoke bar.
The neon-lit warren of alleyways, nightclubs, sex bars, restaurants and karaoke clubs in Tsimshatsui, Mong Kok and Wanchai creates the perfect backdrop for gang warfare.
CRACKDOWN ON CASINO RACKETEERING
McNicol plays down the scale of the triad problem, noting that triads account for only 4.5 percent of Hong Kong crime. "Macau is another story but Hong Kong has been quiet in recent months."
A crackdown on racketeering in casinos in neighbouring Portuguese-ruled Macau sparked a wave of gangster war and violent crime in December.
The violence culminated in an assassination attempt when Macau's top casino police officer was shot as he got out of his car. Shootings and grenade bombings have become commonplace.
Macau returns to Chinese rule in 1999, Hong Kong at midnight on June 30 this year.
Macau's economic recession has reached the triads, and that is why they have become more violent, one source said.
"The cake is getting smaller but the number of people trying to get a piece of it is getting bigger," another told Reuters,
TIED BY OATHS OF BLOOD

The word triad is of English coinage, derived from the sacred emblem of a society, a triangle whose three sides symbolise the powers of Heaven, Earth and Man. In Chinese the names of triad groups usually comprise two or three characters ending with a word meaning "society", "association" or "lodge".
Historically, they were secret societies whose members were tied by oaths of blood, who vowed to drive out foreign invaders and restore the power of their ancient ruling house.
In Hong Kong from its earliest days, they have shown a deadly potential during political emergencies or disturbances.
In 1847, when the British garrison in Hong Kong was sapped of its strength by sending troops to China, local societies exploited the weakness to launch armed attacks on the colony.
The societies were involved in the late 19th century turmoil in China that led to the overthrow of the last imperial dynasty in 1911.
MODERN CRIME GANGS
In modern times, they disintegrated into hundreds of societies all claiming to belong to the triad family but acting independently and often in armed conflict with each other.

Before the communist takeover of the mainland in 1949, rival triads waged turf wars in China's cities, mostly Shanghai, for control of vice rackets attached to gambling, prostitution and drugs. The atmosphere was popularised in a recent film, "Shanghai Triad", starring Chinese screen goddess Gong Li.
Their bread and butter is extortion of protection fees from the entertainment and public transport industries, prostitution, loansharking and drugs.
"They're parasites. They'll threaten restaurants, demand money for protection and then move on," said McNicol.
Today's triads use only the flimsiest remnants of the rituals of the ancient triads, such as initiation oaths which are sworn while burning yellow joss paper.
"These days the ceremonies are very quick. A bit of wine or chicken blood may be spilled. That's all," said McNicol.
HIDDEN HAND
In 1956, a political riot in Hong Kong's Kowloon district was fanned by triads, unleashing anarchy and bloodshed which the authorities were able to crush only by using firearms.
Some in Hong Kong say triads were a hidden hand behind anti-British riots in the 1960s which were ostensibly a spillover from China's Maoist Cultural Revolution.

"We're not worried about triads becoming involved in political disturbances. We monitor them closely," McNicol said, adding there was also no concern that they could destabilise Hong Kong during the transition to Chinese rule.
"If there is violence it's usually among the triad groups themselves with choppings and knifings and it rarely spills over to the general population," McNicol said.
